passages.old: WHAT IS BEST SOCIETY? ''Society*' is an ambiguous term; it may mean mudi or nothing. Every human being, ^unless dwelling alone in a cave, ^i^ a member of society of one sort or another, and therefore it is well to define what is to be understood by the term "Best Society" and why its authority is recognized. Best Society abroad is always the oldest aristocracy; composed not so much of persons of title, which may be new, as of those families and communities which have for the longest period of time known highest cultivation.

Our own Best Society is represented by social groups which have had, since this is America, widest rather than longest association with old world cultivation. Cultivation is always the basic attribute of Best Society, much as we hear in this country of an "Aristocracy of wealth." To the general public a long purse is synonymous with high position, a theory dear to the heart of the "yellow" press and eagerly fostered in the preposterous social functions of screen drama. It is true that Best Society is comparatively rich; it is true that the hostess of great wealth, who constantly and lavishly entertains, will shine, at least to the readers of the press, more brilliantly than her less affluent sister.

Yet the latter, through her quality of birth, her poise, her inimitable distinction, is often the jewel of deeper water in the social crown of her time. The most advertised commodity is not always intrinsically the best, but is sometimes merely the product of a company with plenty of money to spend on advertising. In the same way, money brings certain people before the public, sometimes they are persons of "quality," quite as often •2 . ETIQUETTE * the soKralled '^society leaders" featured in the public press do not belong to good society at all, in spite of their many published photographs and the energies of their pressagents.

Or possibly they do belong to "smart" society; but if too much advertised, instead of being the "queens" they seem, they might more accurately be classified as the court jesters of to-day. New York, more than any city in the world, unless it be Paris, loves to be amused, thrilled and surprised all at the same time; and will accept with outstretched hand any one who can perform this astounding feat. Do not underestimate the ability that can achieve it: a scintillating wit, an arresting originality, a talent for entertaining that amounts to genius, and gold poured literally like rain, are the least requirements.

Puritan America on the other -hand demanding, as a ticket of admission to her Best Society, the qualifications of birth, manners and cultivation, clasps her hands tight across her slim trim waist and announces severely that New York's because Puritan America, as well as the general public, mistakes the jester for the queen. As a matter of fact. Best Society is not at all like a court with an especial queen or king, nor is it confined to any one place or group, but might better be described as an unlimited brotherhood which spreads over the entire surface of the globe, the members of which are invariably people of cultivation and worldly knowledge, who have not only perfect manners but a perfect manner.

Manners are mad« up of trivialities of deportment which can be easily learned if one does not happen to know them; manner is personality, the outward manifestation of one's innate character and attitude toward life. A gentleman, for instance, will never be ostentatious or overbearing any more than he will ever be servile, because these attributes never animate the impulses of a well-bred person. A man whose manners suggest the WHAT IS BEST SOCIETY? 3 grotesque is invariably a person of imitation rather than of real position. Etiquette must, if it is to be of more than trifling use, include ethics as well as manners.

Certainly what*one is, is of far greater importance than what one appears to be. A knowledge of etiquette is of course essential to one's decent behavior, just as clothing is essential to one's decent appearance; and precisely as one wears the latter without being self-conscious of having on shoes and perhaps gloves, one who has good manners is equally unself-conscious in the observance of etiquette, the precepts of which must be so thoroughly absorbed as to make their observance a matter of instinct rather than of conscious obedience. Thus Best Society is not a fellowship of the wealthy, nor does it seek to exclude those who are not of exalted birth ; but it is an association of gentle-folk, of which good form in speech, charm of manner, knowledge of the social amenities, and instinctive consideration for the feelings of others, are the credentials by which society the world over recognizes its chosen members. Chapter II

chapters.title: Introductions and the correct form

passages.old: The word "present" is preferable on formal occasions to the word "introduce." On informal occasions neither word is expressed, though understood, as will be shown below. The correct formal introduction is : "Mr. Distinguished, may I present Mr. Young?" The younger person is always presented to the older or more distinguished, but a gentleman is always presented to a lady, even though he is an old gentleman of great distinction and the lady a mere slip of a girl. No lady is ever, except to the President of the United States, a cardinal, or a reigning sovereign, presented to a man.
passages.plain: Use the word present instead of introduce at formal events. At informal events, you do not need to say either word, but people will still understand what you mean. The correct way to do a formal introduction is to say, Mr. Distinguished, may I present Mr. Young? You always present the younger person to the older person or the person with more status. However, you always present a man to a lady. This is true even if the man is old and important and the lady is just a young girl. You never present a lady to a man unless that man is the President of the United States, a cardinal, or a reigning king or queen.

passages.old: The correct introduction of either a man or woman : To the President, "Mr. President, I have the honor ,fopresent Mrs. Jones, of Chicago." To a Cardinal, "Your Eminence, may I present Mrs. Jones?" Much formality of presenting names on lists is gone through beforehand; at the actual presentation an "accepted" name is repeated from functionary to equerry and nothing is said to the King or Queen except: "Mrs. Jones." But a Foreign Ambassador is presented, "Mr. Ambassador, may I present you to Mrs. Jones." INTRODUCTIONS 6 Very few people in polite society are introduced by their formal titles.
passages.plain: Here is how you introduce a man or a woman. When you speak to the President, you say, 'Mr. President, I have the honor to present Mrs. Jones of Chicago.' When you speak to a Cardinal, you say, 'Your Eminence, may I present Mrs. Jones?' People usually check a list of names before the event. During the actual meeting, people repeat the accepted name from one person to the next. When you speak to the King or Queen, you only say, 'Mrs. Jones.' However, when you introduce a Foreign Ambassador, you say, 'Mr. Ambassador, may I present you to Mrs. Jones.' Very few people in polite society are introduced by their formal titles.

passages.old: A hostess says, "Mrs. Jones, may I present the Duke of Overthere?" or "Lord Blank?"; never "his Grace" or "his Lordship." The Honorable is merely Mr. Lordson, or Mr. HoldofEce. A doctor, a judge, a bishop, are addressed and introduced by their titles. The dergy are usually Mister unless they formally hold the title of Doctor, or Dean, or Canon. A Catholic priest is "Father Kelly." A senator is always introduced as Senator, whether he is still in office or not. But the President of the United . States, once he is out of office, is merely "Mr." and not "Ex-president."
passages.plain: A hostess says, 'Mrs. Jones, may I present the Duke of Overthere?' or 'Lord Blank?' You should never say 'his Grace' or 'his Lordship.' You call The Honorable as Mr. Lordson or Mr. HoldofEce. You address and introduce a doctor, a judge, and a bishop by their titles. You usually call a clergy member Mister unless they officially hold the title of Doctor, Dean, or Canon. You call a Catholic priest Father Kelly. You always introduce a senator as Senator even if he is not in office anymore. However, the President of the United States is only called Mr. once he leaves office. You do not call him Ex-president.

passages.old: In the briefer form of introduction commonly used, "Mrs. Worldly, Mrs. Norman," if the two names are said in the same tone of voice it is not apparent who is introduced to whom ; but by accentuating the more important person^s name, it can be made as clear as though the words "May I present" had been used. The more important name is said with a slightly rising inflection, the secondary as a mere statement of fact. For instance, suppose you say, "Are you there?" and then "It is raining 1" Use the same inflection exactly and say, "Mrs.
passages.plain: There is a short way to introduce people. You can say, "Mrs. Worldly, Mrs. Norman." If you say both names in the same tone of voice, it is not clear who is being introduced to whom. You can make it clear by stressing the name of the more important person. This makes it as clear as saying, "May I present." You should say the more important name with a slightly rising tone. You should say the second name like a simple statement of fact. For example, imagine you say, "Are you there?" and then you say, "It is raining." Use that exact same tone. Say, "Mrs.

passages.plain: Are you there? It is raining, Mrs. Worldly. Mrs. Younger! You should introduce an unmarried woman to a married woman unless the married woman is much younger. In fact, you do not need to make a distinction when you introduce two ladies or two gentlemen to each other. You can say, Mrs. Smith, Mrs. Norman. A man is also often introduced. You can say, Mrs. Worldly, Mr. Norman. However, a mother would say something different to a very distinguished man.

The daughter's name is omitted because it is • extremely bad taste (except in the South) to call her daughter y"Miss Mary" to any one but a servant, and on the other hand she should not present a young man to "Mary." passages.plain: If you say, "Edison, my daughter, Mary," you should change it. If your daughter is married, you should say, "My daughter, Mrs. Smartlington." You should leave out her first name. It is in very bad taste to call your daughter "Miss Mary" to anyone except a servant. You also should not introduce a young man to "Mary." The young man can find out her name later. Other ways to introduce her are allowed. Do not say, "Do you not?" Best society always says, "Mrs."

passages.old: Robinson, have you met Mrs. Jones?" "This is my daughter Ellen, Mrs. Jones." These are all good form, whether gentlemen arc introduced to ladies, ladies to ladies, or gentlemen to gentlemen. In introducing a gentleman to a lady, you may ask Mr. Smith if he has met Mrs. Jones, but you must not ask Mrs. Jones if she has met Mr. Smith! or "Mrs. Jones, I want to make you acquainted with Mrs. Smith." Never say: "make you acquainted with" and do not, in introducing one person to another, call one of them INTRODUCTIONS 7 "my cousin", but to pick out a particular person as "rnyJufriend" is not only bad style but, unless you have only one friend, bad manners, as it implies Mrs.
passages.plain: You can say, 'Robinson, have you met Mrs. Jones?' or 'This is my daughter Ellen, Mrs. Jones.' These are all correct ways to introduce people. This applies whether you are introducing a man to a woman, a woman to a woman, or a man to a man. When you introduce a man to a woman, you can ask Mr. Smith if he has met Mrs. Jones. However, you must not ask Mrs. Jones if she has met Mr. Smith. You must also not say, 'Mrs. Jones, I want to make you acquainted with Mrs. Smith.' Never use the phrase 'make you acquainted with.' When you introduce one person to another, do not call one of them 'my cousin.' You can pick out a specific person as 'my friend.' Calling someone 'my friend' is bad style. It is also bad manners unless you have only one friend because it implies Mrs. Jones is your only friend.

passages.old: Smith is "my friend" and you are a stranger. You may very properly say to Mr. Smith "I want you to meet Mrs. Jones," but this is not a form of introduction, nor is it to be said in Mrs. Jones' hearing. Upon leading present Mr. Smith" or "Mrs. Jones; Mr. Smith." Under no circumstances whatsoever say "Mr. Smith meet Mrs. Jones," or "Mrs. Jones meet Mr. Smith." Either wording is equally preposterous. Most people of good taste very much dislike being asked their names. To say "What is your name?" is always abrupt and unflattering.
passages.plain: Smith is your friend and you do not know the other person. You can say to Mr. Smith, "I want you to meet Mrs. Jones." However, this is not a formal introduction. You must not say this while Mrs. Jones is listening. Instead, you should say, "Present Mr. Smith" or "Mrs. Jones, Mr. Smith." You must never say, "Mr. Smith meet Mrs. Jones" or "Mrs. Jones meet Mr. Smith." Both of those ways of speaking are ridiculous. Most people with good taste do not like being asked for their names. Asking, "What is your name?" is always rude and insulting.

passages.old: If you want to know with whom you have been talking, you can generally find a third person later and ask "Who was the lady with the grey feather in ^ her hat?" The next time you see her you can say "How always shake hands. When a gentleman is introduced to a lady, she sometimes puts out her hand, especially if he is some one she has long heard about from friends in common, but to an entire stranger she generally merely bows her head slightly and says: "How do you do!"
passages.plain: You can find out who you spoke to by asking a third person later. You can ask them who the lady with the grey feather in her hat was. The next time you see her, you can shake her hand. A lady sometimes puts out her hand when a gentleman is introduced to her. She does this especially if she has heard about him from mutual friends. To a complete stranger, she usually just bows her head slightly and says, "How do you do!"

passages.old: Strictly speaking, it is always her place to offer her hand or not as she chooses, but if he puts out his hand, it is rude on her part to ignore it. Nothing could be more ill-bred than to treat curtly any overture made in spontaneous friendliness. No thoroughbred lady would ever refuse to shake any hand that is honorable, not even the hand of a coal heaver at the risk of her fresh white glove. Those who have been drawn into a conversation do not usually shake hands on parting.
passages.plain: You can choose whether or not to offer your hand. However, if a man offers his hand to you, it is rude for you to ignore it. It is very bad manners to be short with someone who is being friendly. A high-class lady would never refuse to shake a hand from an honorable person. She would even shake the hand of a coal heaver even if it risked her clean white glove. People who are just having a conversation do not usually shake hands when they say goodbye.

passages.old: But there is no fixed rule. 8 ETIQUETTE A lady sometimes shakes hands after talking ^th a casual stranger; at other times she does not offer her hand on parting from one who has been punctiliously presented to her. She may find the former sympathetic and the latter very much the contrary. Very few rules of etiquette are inelastic and none more so than the acceptance or rejection of the strangers you meet. There is a wide distance between rudeness and reserve. You can be courteously polite and at the same time extremely aloof to a stranger who does not appeal to you, or you can be welcomingly friendly to another whom you like on sight.
passages.plain: There is no fixed rule. A lady sometimes shakes hands after talking with a casual stranger. At other times she does not offer her hand when leaving someone who was formally introduced to her. She may find the first person friendly and the second person not friendly at all. Very few rules of etiquette are strict. None are more flexible than whether you accept or reject the strangers you meet. There is a big difference between being rude and being reserved. You can be polite but very distant to a stranger you do not like. You can also be very friendly to another person whom you like immediately.

passages.old: Individual temperament has also to be taken into consideration: one person is naturally austere, another genial. The latter shakes hands far more often than the former. As already said, it is unforgivably rude to refuse a proffered hand, but it is rarely necessary to offer your hand if you prefer not to. Best Society has only one phrase in acknowledgment of an introduction: "How do you do?" It literally accepts no other. When Mr. Bachelor says, **Mrs. Worldly, may I present Mr. Struthers?" Mrs. Worldly says, **How do )r you do?"
passages.plain: You must also consider a person's personality. Some people are naturally serious. Others are friendly. Friendly people shake hands much more often than serious people. It is very rude to refuse a handshake if someone offers it to you. However, you do not have to offer your hand if you do not want to. In high society, there is only one phrase to use when someone is introduced to you. That phrase is "How do you do?" It is the only correct response. If Mr. Bachelor says to Mrs. Worldly, "Mrs. Worldly, may I present Mr. Struthers?" Mrs. Worldly says, "How do you do?"

passages.old: Struthers bows, and says nothing. To sweetly is not good form. Saccharine chirpings should be classed with crooked little fingers, high hand-shaking and other affectations. All affectations are bad form. Persons of position do not say: "Charmed," or "Pleased to meet you," etc., but often the first remark is the bepnning of a conversation. For instance. Young Struthers is presented to Mrs. Worldly. She smiles and perhaps says, "I hear that you are going to be in New York all winter?" Struthers answers, "Yes, I am at the Columbia Law School," etc., or since he is much younger than she, he might answer, "Yes, Mrs.
passages.plain: Struthers bows and says nothing. It is not good manners to be too sweet. You should treat overly sugary voices like crooked fingers, high handshakes, and other fake behaviors. All fake behaviors are bad manners. Important people do not say phrases like Charmed or Pleased to meet you. Instead, their first remark is usually the start of a conversation. For example, young Struthers is introduced to Mrs. Worldly. She smiles and might say, I hear that you are going to be in New York all winter? Struthers answers, Yes, I am at the Columbia Law School. Because he is much younger than she is, he might also answer, Yes, Mrs.

passages.old: Worldly," especially if his answer would otherwise be a curt yes or no. Otherwise he does not continue repeating her name. INTRODUCTIONS 9 After an introduction, when you have talked for some time to a stranger whom you have found agreeable, and you then take leave, you say, "Good-by, I am very glad to soon", or **some.time." The other person answers, "Thank ^ you" is all that is necessary. In taking leave of. a group of strangers, it makes no difference whether you have been introduced to them or merely included in their conversation, ^you bow "goodby" to any who happen to be looking at you, but you do not attempt to attract the attention of those who are una- ^ ware that you are turning away.
passages.plain: You should be polite, especially if your answer would otherwise be a short yes or no. You do not keep repeating her name. After an introduction, you may talk for a while with a stranger who seems pleasant. When you leave, you say, "Good-by, I am very glad to see you soon" or "Good-by, I am very glad to see you sometime." The other person only needs to say, "Thank you." When you leave a group of strangers, it does not matter if you were introduced to them or just included in their conversation. You bow good-by to anyone who happens to be looking at you. You do not try to get the attention of people who do not know you are leaving.

Let us suppose you are the hostess: your position is not necessarily near, but it is toward the door. Mrs. King is sitting quite close to you, Mrs. Lawrence also near. Miss Robinson and Miss Brown are much farther away. Mrs. Jones enters. You go a" few* steps forward and shake hands with her, then stand aside as it were, for a second only, to see if Mrs.
passages.plain: You never do this at formal events with many people. At a small lunch, the hostess always introduces guests to each other. Imagine you are the hostess. You do not have to sit right next to everyone, but you should sit near the door. Mrs. King is sitting very close to you. Mrs. Lawrence is also near you. Miss Robinson and Miss Brown are much farther away. Mrs. Jones enters the room. You walk a few steps forward and shake her hand. Then you stand aside for just one second to see if Mrs. Jones will speak.

If Mrs. King is an elderly lady, and Mrs. Jones a young one, Mrs. King merely extends her hand and does not rise. Having said "Mrs. Jones" once, you do not repeat it immediately, but turning to the other lady sitting near you, you say, "Mrs. Lawrence," then you look across the room and continue, "Miss Robinson, Miss Browti, Mrs.
passages.plain: Jones goes to speak to someone. If she does not seem to know anyone, you should stand up if you are nearby. You shake hands with Mrs. Jones and then sit down again. If Mrs. King is an older lady and Mrs. Jones is a young lady, Mrs. King only holds out her hand. She does not stand up. You say the name Mrs. Jones once. Do not say it again right away. Turn to the other lady sitting near you and say Mrs. Lawrence. Then look across the room. Continue by saying Miss Robinson, Miss Browti, and Mrs.

passages.old: Jones !" Mrs. Lawrence, if she is young, rises and shakes hands with Mrs. Jones, and the other two bow but do not rise. At a very big luncheon you would introduce Mrs. Jones 10 ETIQUETTE to Mrs. King and possibly to Mrs. Lawrence, so that Mrs. Jones might have some one to talk to. But if other guests come in at this moment, Mrs. Jones finds a place for herself and after a pause, falls naturally into conversation with those she is next to, without giving her name or asking theirs.
passages.plain: If Mrs. Lawrence is young, she stands up and shakes hands with Mrs. Jones. The other two people bow but they do not stand up. At a very large lunch, you would introduce Mrs. Jones to Mrs. King and maybe to Mrs. Lawrence. You do this so that Mrs. Jones has someone to talk to. If other guests enter at that moment, Mrs. Jones finds a place for herself. After a short pause, she starts a conversation naturally with the people next to her. She does not give her name or ask for their names.

passages.old: A friend's roof is supposed to be an introduction to those it shelters. In Best Society this is always recognized if the gathering is intimate, such as at a luncheon, dinner or house party; but it is not accepted at a ball or reception, or any ^'general" entertainment. People always talk to their neighbors at table whether introduced or not. It would be a . breach of etiquette not to! But if Mrs. Jones and Mrs. Norman merely spoke to each other for a few moments, in the drawing-room, it is not necessary that they recognize each other afterwards.
passages.plain: A friend's roof is meant to introduce you to the people who live there. In high society, this is expected at small gatherings like luncheons, dinners, or house parties. It is not expected at balls, receptions, or any general entertainment. You should always talk to the people sitting next to you at a table even if you have not been introduced. It would be a mistake not to do so. However, if Mrs. Jones and Mrs. Norman only spoke to each other for a few moments in the drawing room, they do not have to recognize each other later.

passages.old: New York's bad manners are often condemned and often very deservedly. Even though the cause is carelessness rather than intentional indifference, the indifference is no less actual and the rudeness inexcusable. It is by no means unheard of that after sitting at table next to the guest of honor, a New Yorker will meet her the next day with utter unrecognition. Not because the New Yorker means to **cut" the stranger or feels the slightest unwillingness to continue the acquaintance, but because few New Yorkers possess enthusiasm enough to make an effort to remember all the new faces they come in contact with, but allow all those who are not especially **fixed" in their attention, to drift easily out of mind and recognition.
passages.plain: People often criticize the bad manners of New Yorkers. This criticism is often deserved. New Yorkers are often rude because they are careless rather than because they mean to be. However, their rudeness is still inexcusable. It happens sometimes that a New Yorker sits next to the guest of honor at a table. The next day, that New Yorker might act like they do not know the person at all. The New Yorker does not mean to ignore the stranger. They do not feel unwilling to stay friends. It is just that few New Yorkers have enough energy to remember every new face they meet. They let people drift out of their minds if those people do not stay in their constant attention.

passages.old: It is mortifyingly true; no one is so ignorantly indifferent to everything outside his or her ow*n personal concern as the socially fashionable New Yorker, unless it is the Londoner ! The late Theodore Roosevelt was a brilliantly shining exception. And, of course, and happily, there are other men and women like him in this. But there are also enough of the snail-in-shell variety to give color to the very just resentment that those from other and more gracious cities hold against New Yorkers. INTRODUCTIONS 11 Everywhere else in the world (except London), the im-* pulse of self-cultivation, if not the more generous ones of consideration and hospitality, induces people of good breeding to try and make the effort to find out what manner of mind, or experience, or talent, a stranger has; and to remember, at least out of -courtesy, anyone for whose benefit a friend of theirs gave a dinner or luncheon.
passages.plain: It is embarrassing but true. Most fashionable New Yorkers do not care about anything outside of their own personal lives. The only people who are as indifferent are people from London. Theodore Roosevelt was a great exception to this rule. Happily, there are other people like him today. However, there are also many people who stay hidden like snails in shells. This gives people from other cities a reason to feel annoyed with New Yorkers. In every other city in the world except London, people with good manners try to learn about others. They want to know a stranger's thoughts, experiences, or talents. They also try to remember the names of people who attended a dinner or lunch hosted by their friends. They do this as a matter of courtesy.

passages.old: To fashionable New York, however, luncheon was at one-thirty; at three there is something else occupying the moment, that is all. Nearly all people of the Atlantic Coast dislike general introductions, and present people to each other as little as possible. In the West, however, people do not feel comfortable in a room full of strangers. Whether or not to Introduce people therefore becomes not merely a question of propriety, but of consideration for local custom. The question as to when introductions should be made, or not made, is one of the most elusive points in the entire range of social knowledge. **Whenever necessary to bridge an awkward situation," is a definition that is exact enough, but not very helpful or clear.
passages.plain: In fashionable New York, lunch is at 1:30. Something else happens at 3:00. Most people on the Atlantic Coast do not like general introductions. They try to introduce people as little as possible. In the West, people do not feel comfortable in a room full of strangers. You must decide whether to introduce people based on local customs. This is not just about what is proper. It is about being thoughtful of local habits. Knowing when to make introductions is one of the hardest parts of social rules. One definition says you should do it whenever you need to fix an awkward situation. This definition is accurate but it is not very helpful or clear.

passages.old: The hostess who allows a guest to stand, awkward and unknown, in the middle of her drawing-room is no worse than she who pounces on every chance acquaintance and drags unwilling victims into forced recognition of each other, everywhere and on all occasions. The fundamental rule never to introduce unnecessarily brings up the question : WHICH ARE THE NECESSARY OCCASIONS? First, in order of importance, is the presentation of everyone to guests of honor, whether the "guests" are distinguished strangers for whom a dinner is given, or a bride and groom, or a debutante being introduced to society.
passages.plain: A hostess who lets a guest stand alone and awkward in her living room is just as bad as a hostess who forces everyone to meet. The rule is that you should never introduce people unless it is necessary. You might wonder which occasions are necessary. The most important task is to introduce everyone to the guests of honor. These guests of honor could be important strangers at a dinner. They could also be a bride and groom. They could also be a debutante being introduced to society.

passages.old: It is the height of rudeness for anyone to go to an entertainment given in honor of some one and fail to "meet" him. (Even though one's memory is too feeble to remember him afterward!) 12 ETIQUETTE * INTRODUCTIONS AT A DINNER The host must always see that every gentleman either knows or is presented to the lady he is to "take in" to dinner, and also, if possible, to the one who is to sit at the other side of him. If the latter introduction is overlooked, people sitting next each other at table nearly always introduce themselves.
passages.plain: It is very rude to go to a party for someone and not meet them. This is true even if you forget them later. The host must make sure every man knows the woman he is taking to dinner. The host must also try to introduce him to the person sitting on his other side. If the host forgets this second introduction, the people sitting next to each other should introduce themselves.

passages.old: A gentleman says, **How do you do, Mrs. Jones. I am Arthur Robinson." Or showing her his place card, "I have to introduce myself, this is my name." Or the lady says first, "I am Mrs. Hunter Jones." And the man answers, "How do you do, Mrs. Jones, my name is Titherington Smith." It is not unusual, in New York, for those placed next each other to talk without introducing themselves, particularly if each can read the name of the other on the place cards. Even in New York's most introductionless circles, people always introduce: A small group of people who are to sit together anywhere.
passages.plain: A man says, How do you do, Mrs. Jones. I am Arthur Robinson. Or he shows her his place card and says, I have to introduce myself, this is my name. Or the lady speaks first and says, I am Mrs. Hunter Jones. Then the man answers, How do you do, Mrs. Jones, my name is Titherington Smith. In New York, it is common for people sitting next to each other to talk without introducing themselves. This happens especially if they can both read the names on the place cards. Even in New York circles where people do not introduce themselves often, people always introduce a small group of people who are going to sit together anywhere.

passages.old: Partners at dinner. The guests at a house party. Everyone at a small dinner or luncheon. The four whp are at the same bridge table. Partners or fellow-players in any game. At a dance, when an invitation has been asked for a stranger, the friend who vouched for him should personally present him to the hostess. "Mrs. Worldly, this is Mr. Robinson, whom you said I might bring." The hostess shakes hands and smiles and says: "I am very glad to A guest in a box at the opera always introduces any gentleman who comes to speak to her, to her hostess, unless the latter is engrossed in conversation with a visitor of her own, or unless other people block the distance between so that an introduction would be forced and awkward.
passages.plain: You should introduce people in these situations. These include partners at dinner. Guests at a house party. Everyone at a small dinner or luncheon. Four people at the same bridge table. Partners or fellow players in any game. At a dance, if a friend vouched for a stranger, that friend should personally introduce him to the hostess. You should say, Mrs. Worldly, this is Mr. Robinson, whom you said I might bring. The hostess shakes hands and smiles and says, I am very glad to meet him. A guest in a box at the opera always introduces any gentleman who comes to speak to her to her hostess. You should do this unless the hostess is busy talking to another guest. You should also skip the introduction if other people are blocking the way and would make an introduction feel forced or awkward.

passages.old: INTRODUCTIONS 13 A newly arriving visitor in a lady's drawing-room is not introduced to another who is taking leave. Nor is an animated conversation between two persons interrupted to introduce a third. Nor is any one ever led around a room and introduced right and left. If two ladies or young girls are walking together and they meet a third who stops to speak to one of them, the other walks slowly on and does not stand awkwardly by and wait for an introduction. If the third is asked by the one she knows, to join them, the sauntering friend is overtaken and an introduction always made.
passages.plain: Do not introduce a new visitor to a person who is leaving a lady's drawing room. Do not interrupt a lively conversation between two people to introduce a third person. Never lead someone around a room to introduce them to people on both sides. If two ladies or girls are walking together and a third person stops to talk to one of them, the other person should keep walking slowly. They should not stand there awkwardly and wait for an introduction. If the person who knows the third person asks them to join the group, the walking friend should stop and an introduction must be made.

passages.old: The third, however, must not join them unless Invited to do so. At a very large dinner, people (excepting the gentlemen and ladies who are to sit next to each other at table) are not collectively introduced. After dinner, men in the smoking room or left at table always talk to their neighbors whether they have been introduced or not, and ladies in the drawing-room do the same. But unless they meet soon again, or have found each other so agreeable that they make an effort to continue the acquaintance, they become strangers again, equally whether they were introduced or not.
passages.plain: The third person must not join the others unless they are invited. At a very large dinner, people are not introduced as a group. This does not include the men and women who sit next to each other at the table. After dinner, men in the smoking room or at the table always talk to the people next to them. They do this even if they have not been introduced. Ladies in the drawing room do the same thing. If they do not meet again soon, they become strangers again. This happens whether they were introduced or not. They only stay friends if they meet again soon or if they enjoy each other's company enough to try to stay in touch.

passages.old: Some writers on etiquette speak of **correct introductions" that carry "obligations of future acquaintance," and "incorrect introductions," that seemingly obligate one to nothing. Degrees of introduction are utterly unknown to best society. It makes not the slightest difference so far as any one's acceptance or rejection of another is concerned how an introdtiction is worded or, on occasions, whether an introduction takes place at all. Fashionable people in very large cities take introductions lightly; they are veritable ships that pass in the night. They show their red or green signals, ^which are merely polite sentences and pleasant manners, and they pass on again.
passages.plain: Some writers say there are correct and incorrect ways to introduce people. They say correct introductions create a duty to be friends in the future. They say incorrect introductions do not create any duty. However, high society does not recognize different levels of introductions. It does not matter how a person is introduced or if they are introduced at all. This does not change whether a person accepts or rejects someone else. Fashionable people in big cities do not take introductions seriously. They are like ships passing in the night. They show their signals. These signals are just polite sentences and pleasant manners. Then they move on.

passages.old: When you are introduced to some one for the second time and the first occasion was without interest and long ago, there is no reason why you should speak of the former meeting. If some one presents you to Mrs. Smith for the second 14 ETIQUETTE time on the same occasion, you smile and say "I have already met Mrs. Smith," but you say nothing if you met Mrs. Smith long ago and she showed no interest in you at that time. Most rules are elastic and contract and expand according to circumstances.
passages.plain: You do not need to talk about a past meeting if it happened a long time ago and was not interesting. If someone introduces you to Mrs. Smith for a second time at the same event, you should smile and say that you have already met her. However, you should say nothing if you met Mrs. Smith a long time ago and she did not show any interest in you then. Most rules are flexible. They can shrink or grow depending on the situation.

passages.old: You do not remind Mrs. Smith of having met her before, but on meeting again any one w*ho was brou^t to your own house, or one who showed you an especial courtesy you instinctively say, "I am so glad to see you again." On occasions it happens that in talking to one person you want to include another in your conversation without making an introduction. For instance: suppose you are talking to a seedsman and a friend joins you in your garden. You greet your friend, and then include her by saying, "Mr.
passages.plain: Do not remind Mrs. Smith that you have met her before. However, when you meet someone again who came to your house or who was very kind to you, you should say, "I am so glad to see you again." Sometimes you want to include another person in your conversation without making a formal introduction. For example, imagine you are talking to a seedsman and a friend joins you in your garden. You greet your friend. Then you include her by saying, "Mr.

passages.old: Smith is suggesting that I dig up these cannas and put in delphiniums." Whether your friend gives an opinion as to the change in color of your flower bed or not, she has been made part of your conversation. This same maneuver of evading an introduction is also resorted to when you are not sure that an acquaintance will be agreeable to one or both of those whom an accidental circumstance has brought together. You must never introduce people to each other in public places unless you are certain beyond a doubt that the introduction will be agreeable to both.
passages.plain: Smith suggests that you should dig up the cannas and plant delphiniums instead. Even if your friend does not give an opinion on the color change of your flower bed, she is now part of your conversation. You might also use this trick to avoid an introduction. You do this when you are not sure if an acquaintance will like the people you have met by chance. You must never introduce people to each other in public places. You must be certain that the introduction will please both people.

passages.old: You cannot commit a greater social blunder than to introduce, to a person of position, some one she does not care to know, especially on shipboard, in hotels, or in other very small, rather public, communities where people are so closely thrown together that it is correspondingly diflicult to avoid undesirable acquaintances wbo have been given the wedge of an introduction. INTRODUCTIONS 15 As said above, introductions in very large cities are unimportant. In New York, where people are meeting new faces daily, seldom seeing the same one twice in a year, it requires a tenacious memory to recognize those one hoped most to see again, and others are blotted out at once.
passages.plain: You should not make a big social mistake. Do not introduce a person to someone important if that person does not want to know them. This is especially true on ships, in hotels, or in other small public places. In these places, people are very close together. It is hard to avoid people you do not want to know once you have been introduced to them. Introductions are not important in very large cities. In New York, people meet new faces every day. People often do not see the same person twice in a year. You need a very strong memory to remember the people you want to see again. Other people are forgotten immediately.

passages.old: People in good society rarely ask to be introduced to each other, but if there is a good reason for knowing some one, they often introduce themselves; for instance, Mary Smith says: Mrs. Titherington Smith's daughter." Mrs. Jones says: Your mother and I have known each other since we were children!" Or, an elder lady asks: "Aren't you Mary Smith? I have known your mother since she was your age." Or a young woman says: "Aren't you Mrs. Worldly?" Mrs. Worldly, looking rather freezingly, politely says "Yes" and waits. And the stranger continues, "I think my sister Millicent Manners is a friend of yours."
passages.plain: People in polite society rarely ask to be introduced. However, they often introduce themselves if they have a good reason to know someone. For example, Mary Smith might say, "Mrs. Titherington Smith's daughter." Mrs. Jones might say, "Your mother and I have known each other since we were children." An older lady might ask, "Aren't you Mary Smith? I have known your mother since she was your age." A young woman might say, "Aren't you Mrs. Worldly?" Mrs. Worldly looks a bit cold but politely says, "Yes" and waits. The stranger then continues, "I think my sister Millicent Manners is a friend of yours."

passages.old: Mrs. Worldly at once unbends. "Oh, yes, indeed, I am devoted to Millicent 1 "Oh, of course, Millicent has often talked of you, and of your lovely voice. I want very much to hear you sing some time." These self-introductions, however, must never presumingly be made. . It would be in very bad taste for Alice to introduce herself to Mrs. Worldly if her sister knew her only slightly. A lady who goes to see another to get a reference for a servant, or to ask her aid in an organization for charity, would never consider such a meeting as an introduction, even though they talked for an hour.
passages.plain: Mrs. Worldly relaxes immediately. She says that she is devoted to Millicent. She says that Millicent has talked about you and your lovely voice often. She says she wants to hear you sing sometime. You must never make these types of self-introductions. It would be in very bad taste for Alice to introduce herself to Mrs. Worldly if her sister only knew her slightly. A lady who visits another person to get a reference for a servant or to ask for help with a charity group would not consider that meeting as an introduction. This is true even if they talked for one hour.

passages.old: Nor would she offer to shake hands in leaving. On the other hand, neighbors who are continually meeting, gradually become accustomed they never become acquaintances. 16 ETIQUETTE Let us suppose some one addresses you, and then slightly disconcerted says: "You don't remember me, do you?" The polite thing, unless his manner does not if a few neutral remarks lead to no enlightening topic, and bring no further memory, you ask at the first opportunity who it was that addressed you. If the person should prove actually to be unknown, it is very easy to repel any further advances.
passages.plain: You should not offer to shake hands when you are leaving. Neighbors who see each other often may become used to seeing each other without becoming friends. Imagine someone speaks to you and says, "You don't remember me, do you?" They might seem a bit confused. The polite thing to do is to make a few neutral comments. If these comments do not lead to a clear topic or help you remember the person, you should ask who they are at the first chance. If the person is actually a stranger, it is very easy to stop them from talking to you further.

passages.old: But nearly always you find it is some one you ought to have known, and your hiding the fact of your forgetfulness saves you from the rather rude and stupid situation of blankly declaring: "I don't remember you." If, after being introduced to you, Mr. Jones calls you by a wrong name, you let it pass, at first, but if he persists At a private dance, young men nowadays introduce their men friends to young women without first asking the latter's permission, because all those invited to a lady's house are supposed to be eligible for presentation to everyone, or they would not be there.
passages.plain: You will almost always find that the person is someone you should have known. You should hide the fact that you forgot them. This saves you from the rude and silly situation of saying you do not remember them. If Mr. Jones calls you by the wrong name after you were introduced, let it pass at first. If he keeps doing it, you can address it. At a private dance, young men today introduce their male friends to young women without asking the women first. This is because everyone invited to a lady's house is expected to be okay to meet everyone. If they were not, they would not be there.

passages.old: At a public ball young men and women keep very much to their own particular small circle and are not apt to meet outsiders at all. Under these circumstances a gentleman should be very careful not to introduce a youth whom he knows nothing about to a lady of his acquaintance, or at least he should ask her first. He can say frankly: "There is a man called Sliders who has asked to meet you. I don't know who he is, but he seems decent. Shall I introduce An introduction by letter is far more binding than a casual spoken introduction which commits you to nothing.
passages.plain: At a public ball, young men and women usually stay with their own small group of friends. They do not often meet people outside of that group. In this situation, a gentleman must be careful. He should not introduce a young person he does not know to a lady he knows. At least, he should ask her first. He can say clearly, "There is a man called Sliders who wants to meet you. I do not know who he is, but he seems decent. Shall I introduce him?" An introduction by letter is more binding than a casual spoken introduction. A spoken introduction does not commit you to anything.

passages.old: This is explained fully and example letters arc given in the chapter on Letters. A letter of introduction is handed you unsealed, always. Jt is correct for you to seal it at once in the presence of INTRODUCTIONS 17 its author. You thank your friend for having written it and go on your journey. If you are a man and your introduction is to a lady, you go to her house as soon as you arrive in her city, and leave the letter with your card at her door. Usually you do not ask to see her; but if it is between four and six o'clock it is quite correct to do so if you choose.
passages.plain: The chapter on Letters explains this fully and gives examples. You always receive a letter of introduction unsealed. You should seal it immediately while the person who wrote it is watching. You thank your friend for writing the letter and then continue your journey. If you are a man and your introduction is to a lady, you go to her house as soon as you arrive in her city. You leave the letter and your card at her door. Usually, you do not ask to see her. However, it is correct to ask to see her if it is between four and six o'clock.

passages.old: Presenting yourself with a letter is always a little awkward. Most people prefer to leave their cards without asking to be received. unless the letter is a business one. In the latter case you go to his office, and send in your card and the letter. Meanwhile you wait in the reception room until he has read the letter and sends for you to come into his private office. If you are a woman, you mail your letter of social introduction and do nothing further until you receive an acknowledgment.
passages.plain: Giving someone a letter to introduce yourself is often awkward. Most people prefer to leave their business cards without asking for them to be accepted. This is not true for business letters. In that case, you go to his office. You send in your card and the letter. You wait in the reception room. You wait until he reads the letter and asks you to come into his private office. If you are a woman, you mail your letter of social introduction. You do nothing else until you receive an acknowledgment.

passages.old: If the recipient of your letter leaves her card on you, you in return leave yours on her. But the obligation of a written introduction is such that only illness can excuse her not asking you to her house, either formally or informally. When a man receives a letter introducing another man, he calls the person introduced on the telephone and asks how he may be of service to him. If he does not invite the newcomer to his house, he may put him up at his club, or have him take luncheon or dinner at a restaurant, as the circumstances seem to warrant. Chapter III
passages.plain: If the person who receives your letter leaves their business card for you, you must leave your card for them. Because you were introduced in writing, the person must invite you to their house unless they are sick. This invitation can be formal or informal. When a man receives a letter introducing another man, he calls the new person on the telephone. He asks how he can help him. If the man does not invite the newcomer to his house, he can let him stay at his club. He can also have him eat lunch or dinner at a restaurant depending on the situation. Chapter III.

chapters.why: Understanding the basic principles of hierarchy and respect helps navigate professional and social interactions with confidence.

chapters.title: Greetings and what to say when introduced

passages.old: As explained in the foregoing chapter, the correct formal greeting is: "How do you do?" If Mrs, Younger is presented to Mrs. Worldly, Mrs. Worldly says "How do you do?" If the Ambassador of France is presented the Ambassador likewise say "How do you do?" or merely bow. There are a few expressions possible under other circumstances and upon other occasions. If you have, through friends in common, long heard of a certain lady, or gentleman, and you know that she, or he, also has heard much of you, you may say when you are introduced to meet you at last I" Do not use the expression "pleased to meet you" then or on any occasion.
passages.plain: The correct formal greeting is "How do you do?" If Mrs. Younger is introduced to Mrs. Worldly, Mrs. Worldly says "How do you do?" If the Ambassador of France is introduced to the Ambassador, the Ambassador says "How do you do?" or simply bows. You can use a few other expressions in different situations. If you have heard a lot about a man or woman through friends and you know they have heard a lot about you, you may say "I meet you at last" when you are introduced. Do not use the phrase "pleased to meet you" then or at any other time.

passages.old: And you must not say you are delighted unless you have reason to be sure that she also is delighted to meet you. To one who has volunteered to help you in charitable work for instance, you would say: "It is very good of In business a gentleman says: "Very glad to meet office: "Very glad to see youl" Informal greetings are almost as limited as formal, but not quite; for besides saying "How do you do?" you can say "Good morning" and on occasions "How are On very informal occasions, it is the present fashion to greet an intimate friend with "Hello 1" This seem- GREETINGS 19 ing^y vulgar salutation is made acceptable by the tone in which it is said.
passages.plain: You must not say you are delighted unless you are sure she is also delighted to meet you. For example, you should say, "It is very good of you to help me with this charity work" to someone who volunteered to help you. In business, a gentleman says, "Very glad to meet you" or "Very glad to see you." Informal greetings are almost as limited as formal ones. However, you can say "Good morning" or sometimes "How are you?" on informal occasions. It is currently fashionable to greet a close friend with "Hello." This greeting might seem vulgar, but it is acceptable because of the tone of your voice.

passages.old: To shout "Hul/ow/" is vulgar, but ordinary tone of voice, sound much the same. But remember that the "Hello" is spoken, not called out, and never used except between intimate friends who call each other by the first name. There are only two forms of farewell: "Good-by" and "Good night." Never say "Au revoir" unless you have been talking French, or are speaking to a French person. Never interlard your conversation with foreign words or phrases when you can possibly translate them into English; and the occasions when jOUr mother tongue will not serve are extremely rare.
passages.plain: It is vulgar to shout Hello. A normal speaking voice sounds very similar. Remember that you should speak Hello rather than call it out. You should only use Hello between close friends who call each other by their first names. There are only two ways to say goodbye. These are Good-by and Good night. Do not say Au revoir unless you have been speaking French or you are speaking to a French person. Do not put foreign words or phrases into your conversation when you can translate them into English. The times when your own language will not work are very rare.

passages.old: Very often in place of the over-worn "How do you do," perhaps more often than not, people skip the words of actual greeting and plunge instead into conversation: news with you?" or "What have you been doing lately?" The weather, too, fills in with equal faithfulness. "Isn't would seem that the variability of the weather was purposely devised to furnish mankind with unfailing material for conversation. In bidding good-by to a new acquaintance with whom you have been talking, you shake hands and say, "Goodhas been especially interesting, or who is somewhat of a pei;sonage you say: "It has been a great pleasure to People do not greet each other in church, except at a wedding.
passages.plain: People often skip the formal greeting "How do you do?" instead. They start a conversation right away. They might ask, "Any news with you?" or "What have you been doing lately?" People also talk about the weather very often. It seems like the changing weather was made to give people things to talk about. When you say goodbye to a new person you have been talking to, you shake hands. If the person was very interesting or a famous person, you say, "It has been a great pleasure." People do not greet each other in church unless there is a wedding.

passages.old: At weddings people do speak to friends sitting near them, but in a low tone of voice. It would be shocking to enter a church and hear a babel of voices I Ordinarily in church if a friend happens to catch your eye, you smile, but never actually bow. If you go to a church not your own and a stranger offers you a seat in 20 ETIQUETTE **Thank you." But you do not greet anyone until you are out on the church steps, when you naturally speak to your friends.
passages.plain: You should speak to friends who are sitting near you at weddings. You must use a low voice. It would be shocking to hear many people talking loudly inside a church. If a friend looks at you in a church, you should smile. You should never bow. If you go to a church that is not your own and a stranger offers you a seat, you say thank you. You do not greet anyone until you are outside on the church steps. You can speak to your friends naturally once you are outside.

passages.old: "Hello" should not be said on this occasion because it is too "familiar" for the solemnity of church surroundings. Gentlemen always shake hands when they are introduced to each other. Ladies rarely do so with gentlemen who are introduced to them; but they usually shake hands with other ladies, if they are standing near together. AH people who know each other, unless merely passing by, shake hands when they meet. A gentleman on the street never shakes hands with a lady without first removing his right glove. But at the keeps his glove on.
passages.plain: Do not say Hello on this occasion. It is too casual for a church. Men always shake hands when they meet someone for the first time. Women rarely shake hands with men who are introduced to them. Women usually shake hands with other women if they are standing near each other. People who already know each other shake hands when they meet unless they are just passing by. A man on the street never shakes hands with a woman without taking off his right glove first. He keeps his other glove on.

passages.old: A hands^hake often creates a feeling of liking or of irritation between two strangers. Who does not dislike a "boneless" hand extended as though it were a spray of sea-weed, or a miniature boiled pudding? It is equally annoying to have one's hand clutched aloft in grotesque affectation and shaken violently sideways, as though it were being used to clean a spot out of the atmosphere. What woman does not wince at the viselike grasp that cuts her rings into her flesh and temporarily paralyzes every finger? The proper handshake is made briefly; but there should be a feeling of strength and warmth in the clasp, and, as in bowing, one should at the same time look into the countenance of the person whose hand one takes.
passages.plain: A handshake often makes two strangers feel like they like each other or feel annoyed. Most people do not like a limp hand that feels like seaweed or a soft pudding. It is also annoying when someone holds your hand high in a fake way and shakes it violently from side to side. It feels like they are trying to wipe a spot out of the air. Many women flinch when someone grips their hand so hard that it cuts into their rings and makes their fingers go numb. A proper handshake should be brief. You should still feel strength and warmth in the grip. You should also look at the face of the person whose hand you are taking at the same time.

passages.old: In giving her hand to a foreigner, a married woman always relaxes her arm and fingers, as it is customary* for him to lift her hand to his lips. But by a relaxed hand is not meant a wet rag; a hand should have life even thou^ it be passive. A woman should always allow a GREETINGS 21 man who is only an acquaintance to shake her hand; she should never shake his. To a very old friend she gives a much firmer clasp, but he shakes her hand more than she shakes his.
passages.plain: When a married woman shakes hands with a foreigner, she should relax her arm and fingers. It is the custom for the man to lift her hand to his lips. Her hand should not be limp like a wet rag. It should still have life even though she is not the one moving it. A woman should always let a man who is only an acquaintance shake her hand. She should never shake his hand first. She gives a much firmer grip to a very old friend. However, the man shakes her hand more than she shakes his.

passages.old: Younger women usually shake the hand of the older; or they both merely clasp hands, give them a dropping movemient rather than a shake, and let go. It IS the height of rudeness for young people not to go and shake hands with an older lady of their acquaintance when they meet her away from home, if she is a hostess to whose house they have often gone. It is not at all necessary for either young women or young men to linger and enter into a -conversation, unless the older lady detains them, which she should not do beyond the briefest minute.
passages.plain: Younger women usually shake the hand of older women. Sometimes they just hold hands for a moment and let go without a full shake. It is very rude for young people to skip shaking hands with an older lady they know. This is especially true if they meet her away from home and she is a hostess they have visited often. Young men and young women do not need to stay and talk. They can leave unless the older lady asks them to stay. If she does ask them to stay, she should not keep them for more than a minute.

passages.old: Older ladies who are always dragging young men up to unprepossessing partners, are studiously avoided and with reason; but otherwise it is inexcusable for any youth to fail in this small exaction of polite behavior, if a young man is talking with some one when an older lady enters the room, he bows formally from where he is, as it would be rude to leave a young girl standing alone while he went up to speak to Mrs. Worldly or Mrs. Toplofty. But a young girl passing near an older lady can easily stop for a moment, say "How do you People do not cross a room to speak to any one unless, to show politeness to an acquaintance who is a stranger there ; to speak to an intimate friend ; or to talk to some one about something in particular. Chapter IV
passages.plain: You should avoid older ladies who always try to introduce young men to partners who are not attractive. However, you must follow a specific rule of polite behavior. If a young man is talking to someone and an older lady enters the room, he must bow from where he is standing. It is rude for him to leave a young girl alone to go speak to a woman like Mrs. Worldly or Mrs. Toplofty. A young girl passing near an older lady can stop for a moment. You should not cross a room to speak to anyone unless you are showing politeness to an acquaintance who is a stranger there. You should also only cross the room to speak to an intimate friend or to talk to someone about a specific topic.

chapters.why: It provides timeless guidance on choosing appropriate language based on the level of formality and the specific social context.

chapters.title: Salutations of courtesy when a gentleman takes off his hat

passages.old: A gentleman takes off his hat and holds it In his hand when a lady enters the elevator in which he is a passenger, but he puts it on again in the corridor. A public corridor is like the street, but an elevator is suggestive of a room, and a gentleman does not keep his hat on in the presence of ladies in a house. This is the rule in elevators in hotels, clubs and apartments. In office buildings and stores the elevator is considered as public a place as the corridor.

What is more, the elevators in such business structures are usually so crowded that the only room for a man's hat is on his head. But even under these conditions a gentleman can reveal his innate respect for women by not permitting himself to be crowded too near to them. When a gentleman stops to speak to a lady of his acquaintance in the street, he takes his hat off with his left hand, leaving his right free to shake hands, or he takes it off with his right and transfers it to his left.

If he has a stick, he puts his stick in his left hand, takes off his hat with his right, transfers his hat also to his left hand, and g^ves her his right. If they walk ahead together, he at once puts his hat on ; but while he is standing in the street talking to her, he should remain hatless. There is no rudeness greater than for him to stand talking to a lady with his hat on, and a cigar or cigarette in his mouth. A gentleman always rises when a lady comes into a room.

In public places men do not jump up for every strange woman who happens to approach. But if any woman addresses a remark to him, a gentleman at once rises to his feet as he answers her. In a restaurant, when a lady bows to him, a gentleman merely makes the gesture of rising by getting up half way from his chair and at the same time bowing. Then he sits down again. When a lady goes to a gentleman's office on business ] he should stand up to receive her, offer her a chair, and not sit down until after she is seated.

When she rises to leave, he must get up instantly and stand until she has left the office. It is not necessary to add that every American citizen stands with his hat off at the passing of the "colors" and When the national anthem is played. If he didn't, some other more loyal citizen would take it off for him. Also every man should stand with his hat off m the presence of a funeral that passes close or blocks his way. A GEIiTLEMAN UFTS HIS HAT Lifting the hat is a conventional gesture of politeness shown to strangers only, not to be confused with bowing, which is a gesture used to acquaintances and friends.

In lifting his hat, a gentleman merely lifts it slightly off his forehead and replaces it; he does not smile nor bow, nor even look at the object of his courtesy. No gentleman ever subjects a lady to his scrutiny or his apparent observation. If a lady drops her glove, a gentleman should pidc it up, hurry ahead of her, on no account nudge her, offer the glove to her and say: "I think you dropped this I" The lady replies: "Thank you." The gentleman should then lift his hat and turn away.

If he passes a lady in a narrow space, so that he blocks her w:ay or in any manner obtrudes upon her, he lifts his hat as he passes. If he gets on a street car and the car gives a lurch just as he is about to be seated and throws him against another passenger, he lifts his hat and says "Excuse me I" He must not take a seat if there are ladies standing. But if he is sitting and ladies enter, should they be young. 24 ETIQUETTE he may with perfect propriety keep his seat.

If a very old woman, or a young one carrying a baby, enters the car, a gentleman rises at once, lifts his hat slightly, and says: "Please take my seat." He lifts his hat again when she thanks him. If the car is very crowded when he wishes to leave it through, please?" As she makes room for him to pass, lifts his hat to another gentleman who offers her a seat, picks up something she has dropped, or shows her any civility. He lifts his hat if he asks anyone a question, and always, if, when walking on the street with either a lady or a gentleman, his companion bows to another person.

In other words, a gentleman lifts his hat whenever he says "Excuse me," "Thank you," or speaks to a stranger, or is spoken to by a lady, or by an older gentleman. And no gentleman ever keeps a pipe, cigar or cigarette in his mouth when he lifts his hat, takes it off, or bows. The standing bow, made by a gentleman wlien he rises at a dinner to say a few words, in response to applause, or across a drawing-room at a formal dinner when he bows to a lady or an elderly gentleman, is usually the outcome of the bow taught little boys at dancing school.

The instinct of clicking heels together and making a quick bend over from the hips and neck, as though the human body had two hinges, a big one at the hip and a slight one at the neck, and was quite rigid in between, remains in a modified form through life. The man who as a child came habitually into his mother's drawing-room when there was "company," generally makes a charming bow when grown, which is wholly lacking in self-consciousness. There is no apparent "heel-clicking" but a camera would show that the motion is there.

In every form of bow, as distinct from merely lifting his hat, a gentleman looks at the person he is bowing to. In a very formal standing bow, his heels come together, his knees are rigid and his expression is rather serious. The informal bow is merely a modification of the above; it is easy and unstudied, but it should suggest the ease of controlled muscles, not the floppiness of a In bowing on the street, a gentleman should never take his hat off with a flourish, nor should he sweep it down to his knee; nor is it graceful to bow by pulling the hat over the face as though examining the lining.

The correct bow, when wearing a high hat or derby. Is to lift it by holding the brim directly in front, take it off merely hi^ enough to escape the head easily, bring it a few indies forward, the back somewhat up, the front down, and put it on again. To a very old lady or gentleman, to show adequate respect, a sweeping bow is sometimes made by a somewhat exaggerated circular motion downward to perhaps the level of the waist, so that the hat's position is upside down. If a man is wearing a soft hat he takes it by the crown instead of the brim, lifts it slightly off his head and puts it on again.

The bow to a friend is made with a smile, to a very intimate friend often with a broad grin that fits exactly with the word "Hello"; whereas the formal bow is mentally accompanied by the formal salutation: "How do The reputation of Southern women for having the gift of fascination is perhaps due not to prettiness of feature more than to the brilliancy or sweetness of their ready smile. That Southern women are charming and "feminine" and lovable is proverbial. How many have noticed 26 ETIQUETTE that Southern women always bow with the grace of a flower bending in the breeze and a smile like sudden sunshine?

The unlovely woman bows as though her head were on a hinge and her smile sucked through a lemon. Nothing is so easy for any woman to acquire as a charming bow. It is such a short and fleeting duty. Not a bit of trouble really; just to incline your head and spontaneously smile as though you thought "Why, there is Even to a stranger who does her a favor, a woman of charm always smiles as she says "Thank you!" As a possession for either woman or man, a ready smile is more valuable in life than a ready wit; the latter may sometimes bring enemies, but the former always brings friends.

Under formal circumstances a lady is supposed to bow to a gentleman first; but people who know each other well bow spontaneously without observing this etiquette. In meeting the same person many times within an hour or so, one does not continue to bow after the second, or at most third meeting. After that ont either looks away or merely smiles. Unless one has a good memory for people, it is always better to bow to some one whose face is familiar than to run the greater risk of ignoring an acquaintance. • THE "CUT DIRECT" For one person to look directly at another and not acknowledge the other's bow is such a breach of civility that only an unforgivable misdemeanor can warrant the rebuke.

Nor without the gravest cause may a lady "cut" a gentleman. But there are no circumstances under which a gentleman may "cut" any woman who, even by courtesy, can be called a lady. On the other hand, one must not confuse absent-mindedness, or a forgetful memory with an intentional "cut." Anyone who is preoccupied is apt to pass others without being aware of them, and without the least want of friendly regard. ' Others who have bad memories forget even those by whom they were much attracted. This does not excuse the bad memory, but it explains the seeming rudeness. A "cut*' Is very different. It is a direct stare of blank refusal, and is not only insulting to its victim but embarrassing to every witness. Happily it is practically unknown in polite society. Chapter V

chapters.title: On the street and in public walking on the street

passages.old: A gentleman, whether walking with two ladies or one, takes the curb side of the pavement. He should never sandwich himself between them. A young man walking with a young woman should be careful that his manner in no way draws attention to her or to himself. Too devoted a manner is always conspicuous, and so Is loud talking. Under no circumstances should he take her arm, or grasp her by or above the elbow, and shove her here and there, unless, of course, to save her from being run overl He should not walk along hitting things with his stick.

The small boy's delight in drawing a stick along a picket fence should be curbed in the nursery I And it is scarcely necessary to add that no gentleman walks along the street chewing gum or, if he is walking with a lady, pufEng a cigar or cigarette. All people in the streets, or anywhere in public, should be careful not to talk too loud. They should especially avoid pronouncing people's names, or making personal remarks that may attract passing attention or give a clue to themselves. One should never call out a name in public, unless it is absolutely unavoidable.

A young girl who was separated from her friends in a baseball crowd had the presence of mind to put her hat on her parasol and lift it above the people surrounding her so that her friends might find her. Do not attract attention to yourself in public. This is one of the fundamental rules of good breeding. Shun conspicuous manners, conspicuous clothes, a loud voice, staring at people, knocking into them, talking across anyone in a word do not attract attention to yourself. Do not expose your private affairs, feelings or innermost thoughts in public.

You are knocking down the walls of your house when you do. Nearly all books on etiquette insist that a "gentleman must offer to carry a lady's bundles." Bundles do not suggest a lady in the first place, and as for gentlemen and bundles I, ^they don't go together at all. Very neat packages that could never without injury to their pride be designated as "bundles" are different. • Such, for instance, might be a square, smoothly wrapped box of cigars, candy, or books. Also, a gentleman might carry flowers, or a basket of fruit, or, in fact, any padcage that lodes tempting.

He might even stagger under bags and suitcases, or a small trunk, ^but carry a "bundle"? Not twice 1 And yet, many an unknowing woman, sometimes a very young and pretty one, too, has asked a relative, a neighbor, or an admirer, to carry something suggestive of a pillow, done up in crinkled paper and odd lengths of joined string. Then she wonders afterwards in unenlightened surprise why her cousin, or her neighbor, or her admirer, who is one of the smartest men in town, never comes to see her any more I To an old lady or to an invalid a gentleman offers his arm if either of them wants his support.

Otherwise a lady no longer leans upon a gentleman in the daytime, unless to cross a very crowded thoroughfare, or to be helped over a rough piece of road, or under other impeding circumstances. In accompanying a lady anywhere at night, whether down the steps of a house, or from one building to another, or when walking a distance, a gentleman always offers his arm. The reason is that in her thin high-heeled slippers, and when it is too dark to see her foothold clearly, she is likely to trip.

Under any of these circumstances when he proffers his 30 ETIQUETTE assistance, he might say: "Don't you think you had better easier if you took my arm along here? The going is pretty bad." Otherwise the only occasions on which a gentleman offers his arm to a lady are in taking her in at a formal dinner, or taking her in to supper at a ball, or when he is an usher at a wedding. Even in walking across a ballroom, except at a public ball in the grand march, it is the present fashion for the younger generation to walk side by side, never arm in arm.

This, however, is merely an instance where etiquette and the custom of the moment differ. Old-fashioned gentlemen still offer their arm, and it is, and long will be, in accordance with etiquette to do so. But etiquette does not permit a gentleman to take In seeing a lady to her carriage or motor, it is quite correct for a gentleman to put his hand under her elbow to assist her; and in helping her out he should alight first and offer her his hand. He should not hold a parasol over her head unless momentarily w'hile she searches in her wrist-bag for something, or stops perhaps to put on or take off her glove, or do anjrthing that occupies both hands.

With an umbrella the case is different, especially in a sudden and driving rain, when she is often very busily occupied in trying to hold "good" clothes out these circumstances, take the gentleman's arm, if the "going" is thereby made any easier. A LADY NEVER "ON THE LEFT" The owner always sits on the right hand side of the rear seat of a carriage or a motor, that is driven by a coachman or a chauffeur. If the vehicle belongs to a lady, she should take her own place always, unless she relinquishes it to a guest whose rank is above her own, such as that of the wife of the President or the Governor. lady the right hand seat.

Whether in a private carriage, a car or a taxi, a lady must never sit on a gentleman's left; because according to European etiquette, a lady "on the left" IS not a "lady." Although this etiquette is not strictly observed in America, no gentleman should risk allowing even a single foreigner to misinterpret a lady's position. It is becoming much less customary than it used to be for a gentleman to offer to pay a lady's way. If in taking a ferry or a subway, a young woman stops to buy magazines, chocolates, or other trifles, a young man accompanjring her usually offers to pay for them.

She quite as usually answers: "Don't bother, I have it I" and puts the change on the counter. It would be awkward for him to protest, and bad taste to press the point. But usually in small matters sucli as a subway fare, he pays a matinee or to tea, he naturally buys the tickets and any rcfresrhment which they may have. Very often it happens that a young woman and a young man who are bound for the same house party, at a few hours' distance from the place where they both live, take the same train, either by accident or by pre-arrangement.

In this case the young woman should pay for every item of her journey. She should not let her companion pay for her parlor car seat or for her luncheon ; nor should he, when they arrive at their destination, tip the porter for carrying her bag. A gentleman who is by chance sitting next to a lady of his acquaintance on a train or boat, should never think of offering to pay for her seat or for anything she may buy from the vendor. THE "ESCORT Notwithstanding the fact that he is met, all dressed in his best store clothes, with his "lady friend" leaning on his arm, in the pages of counterfeit society novels and unauthoritative books on etiquette, there is no such 32 ETIQUETTE actual person known to good society, at least not in New York or any great city, as an escort.

He is not only unknown, but he Is impossible. In good society ladies do not go about under the ''care of gentlemen I It is unheard of for a gentleman to "take" a young girl alone to a dance or to dine or to parties of any description; nor can she accept his sponsorship anywhere whatsoever.
